summary_source_claims.quote: The optimizer seeks a harness that helps the team satisfy the task within B B . It observes public inputs, tool responses, candidate programs, and generated artifacts. It cannot query the official evaluator V V during revision. A host process calls V V after final commitment. A runnable program, completed tool call, or recorded finding does not establish task correctness. Public probes guide revision; official evaluation measures the final outcome.

The coordination component C t C_{t} contains routing flags and contracts for existing handoffs. A contract specifies a version, shared fields, a sender instruction, and a receiver instruction. A planner–coder contract can require observed array dimensions in the handoff. A role procedure can instead require the coder to check its inputs. The former changes handoffs; the latter changes role procedures.

A separate meta-level optimizer invokes the editors, composer, selector, and reflector. These are not executions of the seven-role team. The optimizer’s prompts, validators, selection algorithm, tools, and official evaluator remain outside the editable surface. The controller retains the current harness, task-local lessons L t L_{t} , and traces T t T_{t} . Accepted edits govern later rounds of the same task; they do not become a shared learned harness for later evaluation tasks.

Our shared memory draws on Mycelium’s active context-graph design ( Choudhury et al., 2026 ) . It lets a role retrieve evidence recorded by another role beyond the current handoff. We distinguish graph contents G t G_{t} from a memory policy M t M_{t} . The graph holds observations, interpretations, findings, hypotheses, plans, and unresolved questions. The policy determines what roles record and which records reach them. New findings change G t G_{t} ; retrieval rules belong to M t M_{t} .

The controller executes H t H_{t} to obtain reference evidence o t 0 o_{t}^{0} . Each editor receives the same current harness, task requirements, reference evidence, and retrieved lessons. No editor reads another editor’s proposal. SciMARS has two candidates:

The role editor changes role procedures while preserving coordination. The coordination editor changes at most one existing route or contract while preserving roles. Endpoint guidance belongs to the contract. An editor can retain the harness when evidence does not support change.

The memory editor receives a summary of the available graph and revises recording duties, retrieval filters, query hints, retrieval limits, or subscriptions. It preserves roles and coordination. The validator requires a version increase for changed policies and bounds retrieval limits between zero and twelve. These edits change access to evidence, not the evidence itself.

Probes use isolated workspaces or environment snapshots. Memory-enabled branches start from the same permitted seed and keep their writes separate. A public train–validation probe excludes held-out labels from the graph as well as from model inputs. Earlier live notes cannot enter such a probe if they encode those labels. Candidate probes provide evidence for comparison; stochastic executions do not establish a causal effect from one trial.

For interactive campaigns, the accepted harness governs subsequent live turns; probe artifacts do not replace the team’s acquired data. Composition and retention are distinct decisions. A proposed edit counts as retained only when selection adopts its harness.

Lessons guide the outer editors; the shared graph carries evidence among execution roles. Neither mechanism changes the optimizer itself. A new evaluation task resets adaptation state. A fixed development seed does not transfer evaluation-task updates.

Autonomous Science Bench reports separate GPT-6-Astra and GLM-5.3 cohorts. ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld use z-ai/glm-5.3-flashx , pinned to the Z.AI endpoint through OpenRouter with low reasoning effort and no provider fallback. Within each benchmark and model cohort, method–task runs share the same total model allowance, including execution, edits, probes, and selection.

The discovery evaluation uses experimental-data replay and a digital twin, not new physical wet-lab execution. Computational cost limits our evaluation to the tested language models, DS-STAR-based multi-agent configurations, and subsets of the benchmarks. Future work should evaluate additional base language models and multi-agent systems, as well as more complete benchmark suites, to assess the generality of the framework.

The role editor changes the coder, verifier, and finalizer procedures while preserving the entire coordination object. The coder must use the paths checked in the public trace. The verifier must check numerical output rather than file presence. The finalizer must preserve working code and recheck any rewrite. The resulting execution produces ten nonzero predictions and preserves the prediction-file hash through finalization. Its official mean absolute error (MAE) is 6.17 6.17 , compared with 78.0 78.0 for the round’s reference.

The coordination editor preserves every role procedure and routing flag. It adds one verifier.finalizer contract, which passes verification , code , and execution to the finalizer. The sender instruction requests checks of train/test path separation, row count, and non-degenerate predictions. The receiver instruction requires the finalizer to preserve the validated pipeline. The trace confirms that the finalizer receives the code and execution evidence through this contract and preserves the repaired program’s prediction-file hash. Its official MAE is 11.8 11.8 . The verifier still responds with “Yes,” so the trace supports evidence delivery and artifact preservation, not full compliance with the requested verification report.

items.title: SMO: Compiling Natural Language Skills into Graphs of Reusable State-Move-Outcome Bricks

summary_source_claims.quote: Figure 2 separates reuse compilation from basis evolution. The upper path computes Equation 1 ; the lower path handles uncovered content. Accepted content affects only later frozen snapshots, never the current compilation.
These checks catch omissions, disconnected nodes, unterminated branches, and incomplete results. They establish structural consistency, not semantic equivalence or guaranteed success.

For a possible new operation, the Brick Foundry constructs candidate c c with a complete contract and graph position. Admission requires completeness, novelty, connectivity, verifiability, and plausible reuse:

Incomplete candidates are revised, local differences may remain deltas, and unsupported candidates are rejected. Accepted bricks and retained deltas enter the next frozen snapshot ℬ ( k + 1 ) \mathcal{B}^{(k+1)} without altering ℬ ( k ) \mathcal{B}^{(k)} or current G i G_{i} . Thus only compilation gaps evolve the basis; Agent execution does not feed back.

Representation length is computed from the serialized representation with the same tokenizer implementation pinned in the evaluation code for every condition. It includes only the rawSkill or smoSkill representation, excluding task inputs and execution traces. Runtime token consumption is obtained from execution logs. We first average the five runs of each instance and then report a macro-average over the relevant instances. This metric measures task-execution cost after deployment and excludes the one-time offline cost of compiling skills with SMO.

Evaluation metrics. For each run, an independent GPT-5.5 judge scores the complete execution trace in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] under a fixed rubric. The judge provides semantic scores; deterministic programs check format and constraints and aggregate results. On the fixture corpus, a unit is accepted only when its semantic score meets the pre-specified criterion and every deterministic check succeeds; the criterion is fixed across conditions. We average five run-level scores per skill-conditioned instance and then macro-average over 232 instances. 5/5 Pass requires all five runs to be fully successful and is therefore not pass@5. Better/Tie/Worse compares instance-level averages.

Representation efficiency is reported through the number of shared bricks, total skill-representation tokens, percentage token reduction, and compression ratio. Token reduction is the percentage decrease from the rawSkill representation to the corresponding smoSkill representation, and the compression ratio divides the rawSkill token count by the smoSkill token count. Runtime efficiency is summarized by the average execution tokens per instance and their percentage decrease relative to rawSkill. These quantities are described directly because they are standard ratios rather than new metrics introduced by SMO.

Our evaluation has two main limitations. First, it uses a fixed SkillsBench collection, one executor configuration (GPT-5.5 with Codex-ACP), and a GPT-5.5 judge under a fixed rubric. The Structured Contract comparison uses an internal diagnostic fixture corpus rather than Anything2Skill’s official data or complete system. Results may not transfer directly to other models, harnesses, or skill collections.

Second, SMO does not improve every instance: 24 instances regress from 5/5 Pass to non-5/5, suggesting that compilation may occasionally omit useful details or alter how instructions are interpreted. Moreover, the reported runtime tokens exclude the one-time offline compilation cost, so the overall benefit depends on how frequently compiled skills are reused.

Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable natural-language skills, yet growing skill collections remain accumulations of isolated text artifacts that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose. We argue that the reusable content of a skill lies not in its surface wording but in its procedural transitions: which operation to execute under a given state and which observable outcome to produce. Based on this observation, we propose State–Move–Outcome (SMO), a compilation-like framework that decomposes raw skills into reusable procedural bricks and organizes admitted bricks as an externalized symbolic structure. When compiling a skill, SMO first retrieves and composes existing bricks, dynamically connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure; the candidate becomes reusable only after validation and admission. Experiments on SkillsBench v1.1 demonstrate that SMO represents 232 rawSkills from 87 underlying tasks with 95 shared bricks, reducing the corresponding skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens—a 59.3% reduction and 2.46 × \mathbf{2.46}\times compression . Across 232 skill-conditioned evaluation instances, SMO raises the average task score from 0.6379 to 0.7478 and increases 5/5 Pass instances from 138 to 164 , while matching or outperforming rawSkill on 208 of 232 instances . It also reduces average runtime token consumption by 38.38% . These results show that compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency, and downstream execution.

Table 1 reports corpus-level representation efficiency. The 232 rawSkills contain 366,472 representation tokens in total. SMO compiles them into 232 corresponding smoSkills using 95 shared bricks, reducing the representation to 149,154 tokens. This amounts to a 59.3% reduction and a 2.46 × 2.46\times compression ratio. The comparison measures the token length of functionally corresponding skill representations rather than directly comparing the number of rawSkills with the number of bricks.

summary_override.summary_zh: SMO 把已有自然语言技能编译成可共享的状态、动作与结果单元，并在后续冻结快照中复用获准单元。编译缺口与结构准入检查推动库更新，论文明确说明 Agent 执行不会反馈到这一过程。任务实验评测的是部署后的技能表示，因此记为相关的技能编译与复用工作，不纳入 Harness RSI；运行期节省也未包含离线编译成本。
summary_override.summary_en: SMO compiles existing natural-language skills into shared state, move, and outcome units, retaining admitted units in later frozen compilation snapshots. Compilation gaps and structural admission checks drive library updates; the paper explicitly says Agent execution does not feed back into that process. Its task experiments evaluate deployed skill representations, so this is related skill-compilation and reuse work rather than Harness RSI. Reported runtime savings also exclude offline compilation cost.

summary_source_claims.quote: For a task x x , the Engineer uses evidence e e to sample a proposal trajectory τ E \tau_{\mathrm{E}} . Validation and fallback map it to the executed harness h = 𝒱 ⁡ ( τ E ) h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}}) . The Solver acts under h h , producing trajectory τ S \tau_{\mathrm{S}} and terminal task reward R ⁡ ( x , τ S ) R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}) . For role i ∈ { E , S } i\in\{\mathrm{E},\mathrm{S}\} , θ i \theta_{i} and ϕ i \phi_{i} are actor and critic parameters, with actor policy π θ i \pi_{\theta_{i}} . Indices t t , b b , and k k denote generated-token positions, paired episodes, and saved checkpoints, respectively; θ S ( k ) \theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(k)} and h k h_{k} identify saved weights and code. The no-harness condition ∅ \varnothing retains the base executor.

For a task x x , the Engineer receives historical feedback e e and samples a proposal trajectory τ E \tau_{\mathrm{E}} . Validation and fallback map that proposal to the executed harness h = 𝒱 ⁡ ( τ E ) h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}}) . The Solver then interacts with the environment under h h , producing trajectory τ S \tau_{\mathrm{S}} and task reward R ⁡ ( x , τ S ) R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}) . An invalid proposal maps to h = ∅ h=\varnothing , retaining the base executor.

The same reward trains both policies: the Engineer learns which harnesses support successful execution, while the Solver learns how to complete tasks under those harnesses. Each policy is updated on its own generated outputs, without differentiating through harness execution. We use a KL-regularized SAO-based actor–critic backbone ( Hou et al., 2026 ) , with a fixed reference policy for each role. The local realization retains behavior–proximal token-ratio decoupling.

The Engineer generates a harness once, whereas the Solver acts over multiple turns. Their different output lengths and KL penalties can produce different return scales despite the shared task reward. Writing the raw, unweighted critic target as G i , t G_{i,t} , we normalize critic targets separately for each role:

Solver-only rounds freeze the Engineer’s parameters but still sample fresh harnesses. They use unit partner weights. Thus, the Solver continues learning under sampled harnesses while their generating policy remains fixed.
Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure. At deployment, we select a saved harness and evaluate it with a frozen Solver checkpoint.

Algorithm 1 Joint learning of the Engineer and Solver 0: Engineer and Solver policies, independent critics, reference policies, task/evidence stream 1: for each training round do 2: Choose active roles according to Schedule. 3: Engineer samples a code proposal from historical feedback. 4: Validate it to obtain the executed harness and run the Solver. 5: Record both outputs and their shared task reward. 6: for each active role do 7: Estimate values using Context and ValueNorm. 8: Compute and standardize advantages. 9: Apply Peer weights and update the actor through the SAO-based path. 10: Update the critic on normalized return targets. 11: end for 12: end for 13: Select a saved harness and Solver checkpoint for evaluation.

Except for locally evaluated JoMoHa and WHALE, scores are taken from Harness-R1 ( Shao et al., 2026 ) ; we use its training and test sets, with checkpoint and harness selection on a separate validation set. The task model is Qwen3.5-9B; frontier model names denote harness editors, not replacement Solvers. Agent SFT + Harness-R1 additionally fine-tunes the task model, while WHALE uses its RSFT-plus-search recipe. WHALE alternates after eight environment interactions (16 training steps), uses the same harness-search settings as JoMoHa , and matches its total environment-interaction budget. Section 6.2 examines one-sided learning, frozen-Engineer training, program swaps, and coordination components.

Learning curves alone cannot separate improvements in Solver ability from improvements in the generated runtime. We therefore cross-evaluate saved programs and Solver checkpoints (Table 5 ). At the later Solver, replacing the initial program with the later program raises success from 92.5% to 96.5%, without changing model weights. Relative to no harness, the later program gains 5.0 points, with no observed success-to-failure regressions on this evaluation set. The earlier and later learned programs also both improve the earlier Solver from 91.5% under the initial program to 95.0%. These results show that the saved programs contribute useful behavior beyond the initial runtime, including at a different Solver checkpoint. The equal 95.0% scores on the earlier Solver, but 95.0% versus 96.5% on the later Solver, further show that program value depends on the Solver with which it is paired.

summary_override.summary_zh: JoMoHa 用任务执行回报共同训练生成可执行 Harness 的 Engineer 与执行任务的 Solver。Engineer 根据历史反馈提出代码，经验证后运行；保存的程序与模型检查点经验证集选择，再冻结用于评估，固定 Solver 的新旧程序互换用于区分代码贡献。纳入共演化的依据是模型学习之外确有代码工件生成、保留与复用；不能写成部署期持续自改，也不能把引用的全部基线当作同批重跑。
summary_override.summary_en: JoMoHa trains an Engineer that generates executable harnesses and a task-solving Solver using task outcomes. Historical feedback conditions code proposals, which are validated before execution. Saved programs and model checkpoints are selected on validation and frozen for evaluation; program swaps at fixed Solver weights examine the contribution of the code. Its coevolution evidence includes retained and reused code artifacts beyond model learning, without establishing continual self-modification at deployment or local reruns of every cited baseline.
